about.title: Santa Monica Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Santa Monica's workforce is scattered across hotel kitchens along Pacific Coast Highway, retail floors near 4th Street, tech and media offices, active construction sites, and the steady flow of service vans and delivery trucks using Lincoln Boulevard and the I-10 every shift. Getting hurt in any of those settings usually begins the same way: a workers' compensation claim through your employer, which covers medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of who was at fault. Under California law, that claim is generally your only remedy against the employer itself. It is not always the whole picture, though. If someone outside your company contributed to the injury, such as a subcontractor on a Santa Monica job site, the owner of a building where you were working, the manufacturer of equipment that failed, or another driver who struck your work vehicle, a separate injury claim may exist alongside comp. Santa Monica logged 445 injury collisions in 2025, with 572 people hurt, and some of those were simply people doing their jobs. LawProactive connects you for free with an independent attorney who can tell you which claims fit your situation.

whyChoose.title: Why Santa Monica Workers Use LawProactive

items.title: Comp Is Not Always the Last Word
items.desc: Workers' compensation is typically your exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party, like a subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or another driver, can open a separate injury claim. The attorneys in our network look at both.

items.title: Reporting and Protection From Retaliation
items.desc: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and it is illegal for an employer to punish you for doing so. An attorney can help you document the report and respond if your hours or job suddenly change afterward.

items.title: A Two-Year Clock on Third-Party Claims
items.desc: Any claim against someone other than your employer generally must be filed within two years of the injury. Connecting early gives an independent attorney time to gather evidence from the site or the crash before it disappears.

items.question: I was hit on Lincoln Boulevard while making deliveries for my employer. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were working, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your wages no matter who caused the crash. Because another driver was involved, you may also have a separate injury claim against that driver, which is where the two-year deadline applies. Reported crashes in Santa Monica tend to peak on Fridays between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m., a window when many delivery and service routes are still running.

items.question: Can my Santa Monica employer fire me for reporting an injury?
items.answer: No. California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report an injury or file a workers' compensation claim. You should still report the injury within 30 days to protect your claim. If your schedule, pay, or position changes shortly after you report, note the dates and mention it to the attorney you are connected with.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge me anything to get connected?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free connection service, not a law firm, and we do not charge injured workers. The independent attorneys in our network handle injury claims on contingency, which means there is no fee unless there is a recovery in your case.
